1→/** Article body content for Thoughts pages */
     2→
     3→export const ARTICLE_CONTENT: Record<string, string[]> = {
     4→  "brand-systems": [
     5→    "I've spent the better part of two decades watching brand guidelines gather dust on shelves. Beautifully designed PDFs that no one opens after the first week. The problem isn't that guidelines are wrong -- it's that they're incomplete. They tell you what not to do. They don't tell you how to think.",
     6→    "A brand system is fundamentally different. Where guidelines are a rulebook, a system is a toolkit. It gives your team the building blocks -- color, type, spacing, imagery, tone -- and the logic for combining them. It's the difference between handing someone a recipe and teaching them how to cook.",
     7→    "At GLG, I inherited a brand that had fragmented across 25+ countries and dozens of business units. Everyone had the guidelines. Nobody was following them -- not because they were rebellious, but because the guidelines couldn't answer the questions they were actually asking. How should this investor presentation look? What about a recruitment email? A conference booth in Tokyo?",
     8→    "Guidelines break at the edges. Systems flex. When we rebuilt GLG's visual language, we didn't write more rules. We built a flexible grid, a rationalized color system, and a typography hierarchy that could adapt from pitch decks to product interfaces. Every element earned its place because it solved a recurring problem, not because it looked good in a PDF.",
     9→    "The test of a brand system is what happens when you're not in the room. If the design team in another office, on another continent, can produce work that feels unmistakably on-brand without calling you -- the system is working. If they can't, you don't have a system. You have a style guide and a bottleneck.",
    10→    "The brands that endure -- the ones that feel coherent across every touchpoint -- aren't the ones with the thickest guidelines. They're the ones with the clearest systems. Systems that trust the people using them. Systems that answer 'how' instead of just 'don't.'",
    11→  ],
    12→  "fractional-cd": [
    13→    "Not every company needs a full-time creative director. But every brand needs creative direction. That gap -- between what a brand needs and what it can sustain -- is where fractional creative direction lives.",
    14→    "I spent years leading creative teams in-house at Bloomberg and GLG. The work was deep and rewarding. But I kept noticing something: many of the companies that needed creative leadership the most were the ones that couldn't justify a six-figure salary for it. Startups with brilliant products and terrible brand presence. Mid-size firms outgrowing their DIY identity. Companies in transition who needed a steady hand for twelve months, not twelve years.",
    15→    "Fractional creative direction isn't consulting. Consultants diagnose and leave. A fractional CD embeds. I sit in the design reviews. I know the team's names. I understand why the CEO cares about that particular shade of blue. The difference is duration and commitment -- I'm there for the critical phase, not forever.",
    16→    "The model works because brand-building isn't linear. There are moments that demand intense creative leadership -- a rebrand, a product launch, a merger -- followed by long stretches where a well-built system runs itself. Paying a full-time director to maintain what's already working is like keeping the architect on payroll after the building is done.",
    17→    "What I've found is that the constraint of time actually improves the work. When you know you have six months to build a visual system and train a team to use it, you make sharper decisions. You focus on what matters. You build for independence, not dependence.",
    18→    "The best outcome of a fractional engagement is when the team doesn't need you anymore. That means the system works, the team is confident, and the brand has the foundation it needs to evolve on its own. That's not a failure of retention. That's a success of design leadership.",
    19→  ],
    20→  "visual-storytelling": [
    21→    "B2B doesn't have to be boring. I know -- that sentence itself is almost a cliche at this point. But the reason it keeps getting repeated is that most B2B brands haven't actually internalized it. They've heard the message and then gone right back to stock photography of people shaking hands in front of glass conference rooms.",
    22→    "Visual storytelling in B2B is harder than in consumer brands, and that's exactly what makes it interesting. Consumer brands can lean on lifestyle aspiration, emotional impulse, cultural identity. B2B brands have to make complex, abstract, often technical value propositions feel human and compelling. That's a genuine creative challenge.",
    23→    "At TIAA, we had to tell a story that spanned 30 years of retirement data. Not exactly the stuff of Instagram virality. But the data was genuinely meaningful -- it represented real people's experiences of retirement, their fears and their fulfillment. The design challenge was to honor the seriousness of the data while making it accessible and emotionally resonant.",
    24→    "The solution wasn't to make it 'fun.' It was to make it human. We led with real voices -- retirees talking about what mattered to them. We designed the data visualizations to feel warm rather than clinical. We chose photography that showed real moments, not staged ones. The work succeeded because it respected both the audience's intelligence and their humanity.",
    25→    "The pattern I've seen across two decades of B2B work is this: the brands that communicate most effectively are the ones that stop trying to sound important and start trying to be clear. Clarity is the ultimate storytelling tool. When you strip away the jargon and the stock imagery and the corporate voice, you find something much more powerful -- a straightforward story about how you help people solve real problems.",
    26→    "That's not boring. That's the foundation of every great brand, B2B or otherwise.",
    27→  ],
    28→  "design-leadership": [
    29→    "You don't need to be a director to lead design thinking in your organization. In fact, some of the most impactful design leadership I've witnessed has come from people without the title, the corner office, or the seat at the executive table.",
    30→    "Design leadership isn't about authority. It's about influence. It's the ability to shift how people in your organization think about visual communication, user experience, and brand consistency. And that can happen from any position -- if you're intentional about it.",
    31→    "Early in my career, long before I had 'Director' in my title, I learned that the most effective way to advocate for better design wasn't to critique what existed. It was to show what was possible. When I wanted to change how we approached a project, I didn't write a memo. I made a prototype. I showed, I didn't tell. That's a design principle, but it's also a leadership principle.",
    32→    "The practical reality is this: organizations don't change because someone tells them to. They change because someone demonstrates a better way of working and makes it easy to adopt. If you want your company to take brand consistency seriously, don't send an email about it -- build a template system that makes inconsistency harder than consistency.",
    33→    "Another thing I've learned: design leadership requires translation. You have to speak the language of the people you're trying to influence. With marketing, talk about conversion and engagement. With sales, talk about credibility and differentiation. With the C-suite, talk about brand equity and competitive positioning. The design argument is always there -- you just have to frame it in terms your audience cares about.",
    34→    "The title will come if the leadership is real. But don't wait for the title to start leading. Every presentation you improve, every template you systematize, every creative review where you push for better -- that's design leadership. And the organizations that thrive are the ones with design leaders at every level, not just at the top.",
    35→  ],
    36→};
